plan.topic: EloraTZP (eloralintide + tirzepatide) vs tirzepatide 15 mg in adults with obesity or overweight and type 2 diabetes: phase 2b, 367 adults, 48 weeks, EASD 2026
plan.angle: Title: 'Tirzepatide + Amylin (EloraTZP) vs Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) in Type 2 Diabetes: 23.3% vs 14.8% in Phase 2' (fits the ≤100 character limit). In the first 10 seconds say: top dose, 48 weeks, adults with T2D plus overweight or obesity, small Phase 2b, numerical comparison not formally tested, more people stopped the combo because of side effects. Include placebo figures, show the arm sizes, and set the discontinuation rates side by side from the primary source. Status: investigational, Phase 3 planned (Lilly says by end of 2026). Nothing changes for people on tirzepatide today. End with the exact prescriber line.
plan.working_title: Did Lilly's New Combo Beat Tirzepatide (Mounjaro)? EloraTZP's 23.3% vs 14.8% Explained
plan.why: Top radar momentum (88), low competition, and it's brand-new: there are almost no consumer explainers yet. It fits the headline-decoder format that beat our median, and phase 2b data gives enough depth for 10+ minutes. | fact-check: Core numbers check out against Lilly's EASD 2026 release and the HCPLive write-up. The trial was 48 weeks, 367 adults with obesity or overweight AND type 2 diabetes, run in the US and Argentina, double-blind and placebo-controlled. It had placebo, eloralintide-alone, tirzepatide 15 mg and EloraTZP arms. Baseline was 105.4 kg and A1C 8.1% (≈65 mmol/mol). EloraTZP gave 13.2–23.3% weight loss (23.3% at the top dose) vs 14.8% with tirzepatide 15 mg. Eloralintide alone gave 8.2–12.3%. A1C fell by 2.2–2.9 percentage points vs 2.4 with tirzepatide. Lilly plans Phase 3 of an optimised co-formulation by the end of 2026. Problems to fix: (1) The working title has no population and no 'top dose' / Phase 2 qualifier. It also says 'beat' when no p-values for EloraTZP vs tirzepatide were reported, so they are numerical comparisons, not proven superiority. (2) Dropout rates are a major limit and must be shown with their comparator. HCPLive reports adverse-event discontinuation of 10.8–27.0% for EloraTZP vs 2.9% for tirzepatide (placebo is listed as 16.7%, which looks odd). Take these only from Lilly's primary release or the EASD abstract, and check whether each figure is 'due to adverse events' or overall. (3) With 367 people split across many arms, each arm is roughly 30–40 people. Say this. (4) Report placebo weight loss next to the drug figures, and name the estimand (efficacy vs treatment-regimen) as the primary source does. (5) Never refer to the 'tirzepatide 15 mg' arm as dosing guidance. Phrase it as 'the highest approved tirzepatide dose arm' and don't give titration detail. Amylin context: CagriSema (Novo), petrelintide (Zealand/Roche) and EloraTZP are all investigational as of Sept 2026. Pramlintide is an older approved amylin analogue used with insulin; say so if you claim 'no amylin drug is approved', or avoid that claim.

package.description:
Did eloralintide + tirzepatide (EloraTZP) really beat tirzepatide (Mounjaro) alone? Top dose: 23.3% vs 14.8% weight loss at 48 weeks in adults with type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity. Here's the fine print.

Quick answer: In a 48-week Phase 2b trial of 367 adults with type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity, Lilly's investigational combo EloraTZP averaged 23.3% weight loss at the top dose (13.2–23.3% across combo doses), vs 14.8% for tirzepatide 15 mg alone and 3.0% for placebo. These are Lilly's "if everyone stayed on treatment" estimates. No formal head-to-head test vs tirzepatide has been reported, and 10.8–27.0% stopped the combo because of side effects vs 2.9% on tirzepatide. Lilly plans to start Phase 3 by the end of 2026. EloraTZP isn't approved; the only legitimate way to receive it is inside a clinical trial.

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your own situation. It's a prescription medicine. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

script.working_title: Amylin Combo EloraTZP vs Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) in T2D: 23.3% (Top Dose) vs 14.8%, Phase 2b
script.hook_pattern: Stakes + specificity headline decoder. The first line gives the verified top-dose number with its population, timeframe and placebo figure. Then come caveats that break the pattern: a small Phase 2b trial, no head-to-head test reported, and more people stopping the combo than tirzepatide because of side effects. It ends on an open loop about the detail that matters more than 23.3%, paid off in 'The fine print': 23.3% is the 'if everyone stayed on treatment' estimate, in a trial where up to 27% of a group stopped for side effects.

scenes.narration: Top dose, 48 weeks: Lilly's new combo cut body weight by 23.3% in adults with type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity. Tirzepatide alone: 14.8%. Placebo: 3.0%.

visual.stat_label: Top combo dose vs tirzepatide; placebo 3.0%

scenes.retention_device: Cold open: the verified headline number with its population, comparator and placebo in the first 10 seconds

scenes.narration: But this was a small Phase 2b trial. No formal head-to-head test of that gap has been reported. And more people stopped the combo than tirzepatide because of side effects.
scenes.on_screen_text: Promising, but read the fine print

items: More stopped the combo than tirzepatide

scenes.retention_device: Pattern interrupt: three caveats undercut the headline straight away

scenes.narration: The combo is called EloraTZP. It pairs eloralintide, an experimental drug that acts on amylin receptors, with tirzepatide, the medicine sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound.
scenes.retention_device: Names the thing viewers are searching for

scenes.narration: The results were presented at the EASD 2026 meeting, and the headlines are already loud. So let's decode what these numbers actually show, and what they don't.
scenes.retention_device: Promise: what the viewer will get from the video

scenes.narration: Because by the end, you'll know the one detail that could decide whether that 23.3% holds up in bigger trials. Spoiler: it isn't a weight number.
scenes.retention_device: Main open loop (paid off in 'The fine print')

scenes.narration: First, the new ingredient. To understand why Lilly paired these two drugs, you need to meet a hormone most people have never heard of.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter change with a curiosity gap: a hormone you've never heard of

scenes.narration: It's called amylin. Your pancreas makes it in the very same cells that make insulin, and releases it alongside insulin when you eat.
scenes.retention_device: Visceral 'you' framing: your own body makes it

scenes.narration: Think of amylin as a second 'I'm full' signal. It acts on the brain to help reduce how much you eat, slows how fast your stomach empties, and dampens a blood-sugar-raising hormone called glucagon after meals.
scenes.retention_device: Analogy that makes the mechanism memorable

scenes.narration: GLP-1 is a different gut hormone with some overlapping jobs. Tirzepatide goes a step further: it acts on GLP-1 receptors and on the receptor for a second gut hormone, called GIP.
scenes.retention_device: Builds the 'two signals' setup before the third arrives

scenes.narration: So the idea behind EloraTZP is simple. Add a third signal, through amylin, on top of the two tirzepatide already uses.
scenes.retention_device: Simple payoff of the mechanism setup

scenes.narration: Amylin-based medicine isn't brand new, by the way. Pramlintide, a lab-made version of amylin, was approved in the US back in 2005 for people who use mealtime insulin.

visual.myth: No amylin-based drug has ever been approved
visual.fact: Pramlintide, an amylin analogue, is approved for people using mealtime insulin
visual.stock_query: old calendar page with pill bottle

scenes.retention_device: Surprising historical fact

scenes.narration: What's new is pairing amylin-type drugs with GLP-1-type drugs for weight. Novo Nordisk's CagriSema combines an amylin analogue with semaglutide. EloraTZP is Lilly's take on the idea.
scenes.retention_device: Raises the stakes: a race between two companies

scenes.narration: Which raises the obvious question: does adding amylin really move the needle beyond tirzepatide on its own? Here's how Lilly tested it.
scenes.retention_device: Question to the viewer before the section change

scenes.narration: The trial enrolled 367 adults, all living with type 2 diabetes plus overweight or obesity, at sites in the US and Argentina. It ran for 48 weeks.

visual.stock_query: map with US and Argentina pins

scenes.retention_device: Chapter card with concrete numbers

scenes.narration: It was double-blind and placebo-controlled. Neither the participants nor their study doctors knew who was getting which treatment.
scenes.retention_device: Mini-story about trial design

scenes.narration: People were randomly assigned to placebo, to eloralintide on its own, to tirzepatide at its highest approved dose, or to the EloraTZP combo at several dose levels.
scenes.retention_device: Visual list of the arms the rest of the video compares

scenes.narration: On average, they started at 105.4 kilograms, about 232 pounds, with an A1C of 8.1%, or about 65 mmol/mol.
scenes.retention_device: Concrete baseline numbers

scenes.narration: For comparison, a common A1C goal for many adults with diabetes is below 7%, or 53 mmol/mol. So these were people whose blood sugar still needed work.
scenes.retention_device: Puts the number in context for the viewer

scenes.narration: Now here's the part most headlines skip. 367 people sounds like a big trial. But they were split across 10 different groups.

visual.stock_query: big crowd splitting into small groups

scenes.retention_device: Re-hook: 'the part most headlines skip'

scenes.narration: That works out to roughly 30 to 40 people per group. In a group that size, a handful of people doing unusually well, or dropping out, can shift the average.
scenes.retention_device: Surprising stat that reframes the headline

scenes.narration: And that's normal for a Phase 2b trial. Its main job is usually to find promising doses and spot safety signals, not to prove one drug beats another. That's what Phase 3 is for.

visual.myth: Phase 2 proves which drug is better
visual.fact: Phase 2 usually finds promising doses; Phase 3 tests the comparison

scenes.retention_device: Myth correction the viewer may hold

scenes.narration: So keep that in mind as we look at the number everyone's sharing. Because the full story is more interesting than '23 beats 15.'
scenes.retention_device: Mini-cliffhanger before the section change

scenes.narration: After 48 weeks, people in the EloraTZP groups lost between 13.2% and 23.3% of their body weight on average, depending on the dose.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter card that delivers the range, not just the peak

scenes.narration: The top dose reached 23.3%. The tirzepatide group lost 14.8%.

visual.stat_label: Top combo dose vs tirzepatide; placebo 3.0%

scenes.retention_device: Restates the headline with its 'top dose' label

scenes.narration: Eloralintide on its own, with no tirzepatide, produced 8.2% to 12.3% across its doses. Respectable for a single drug, but clearly below the combo.
scenes.retention_device: New number keeps the comparison moving

scenes.narration: Here's the full lineup side by side. And notice something: the bottom of the combo range, 13.2%, actually sits below tirzepatide alone.
scenes.retention_device: 'Notice something' surprise

scenes.narration: So adding amylin didn't put every combo group ahead of tirzepatide. The headline 23.3% comes from the top dose, not from the combo in general. And that lowest combo paired eloralintide with a lower tirzepatide dose than the tirzepatide-only group got.

visual.myth: Every combo dose lost more than tirzepatide
visual.fact: The 23.3% figure is the top dose; the lowest dose was 13.2%

scenes.retention_device: Corrects the takeaway most headlines imply

scenes.narration: What about placebo? People on placebo lost 3.0% over the same 48 weeks, so every active group did far better than placebo.
scenes.retention_device: Fills in the comparator every number needs

scenes.narration: For context only: SURMOUNT-2 was a large Phase 3 trial in adults with type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity. There, counting people as if they stayed on treatment, people on placebo lost 3.3% over 72 weeks.

visual.stat_label: Placebo, SURMOUNT-2, 72 weeks, 'if stayed on' estimate (separate trial)

scenes.retention_device: Placebo context from a verified trial, on the matching estimand

scenes.narration: And here's a twist. In that same trial, counting people as if they stayed on treatment, the same way this new trial reports its numbers, tirzepatide's highest dose produced 15.7% over 72 weeks. In this new trial, the tirzepatide group reached 14.8% in 48.

visual.stat_label: Tirzepatide, 'if stayed on' estimate: SURMOUNT-2 (72 wk) vs this trial (48 wk)

scenes.retention_device: 'Here's a twist' re-hook that also plants the estimand idea

scenes.narration: Different trials and different people, so you can't compare them directly. But it's at least a sign the tirzepatide group here wasn't a weak comparator.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the twist

scenes.narration: Now, a question for you. Ever noticed that weight-loss numbers from diabetes trials look smaller than the famous ones? There's a reason.
scenes.retention_device: Direct question to the viewer opens a new loop

scenes.narration: In SURMOUNT-1, adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related health problem, but without diabetes, lost 20.9% on tirzepatide's highest dose over 72 weeks, versus 3.1% on placebo, counting everyone randomized.

visual.stat_label: Tirzepatide vs placebo, no diabetes, 72 weeks

scenes.retention_device: Comparison stat that pays off the question

scenes.narration: On the same medicines, people with type 2 diabetes tend to lose less weight. That's why 23.3% in a diabetes population turned heads, even as a top-dose result in a small trial.
scenes.retention_device: Explains why the headline is newsworthy without overselling it

scenes.narration: Another reference point: Novo's CagriSema, also an amylin-plus-GLP-1 combo, produced 13.7% versus 3.4% on placebo over 68 weeks in adults with type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity, in the REDEFINE 2 trial. That figure counts everyone randomized, whether or not they stayed on treatment.

visual.stat_label: CagriSema vs placebo, T2D, 68 weeks (counts everyone)

scenes.retention_device: Rival comparison adds stakes

scenes.narration: Again: different trials, different designs, different lengths, and sometimes different ways of counting. Cross-trial comparisons are a sketch, not a scoreboard.
scenes.retention_device: Memorable one-liner

scenes.narration: But weight is only half the reason people with type 2 diabetes take these medicines. The other half is blood sugar. And this part might surprise you.
scenes.retention_device: Mini-cliffhanger before the section change

scenes.narration: A1C reflects your average blood sugar over roughly the past 3 months. Remember, these participants started at 8.1%.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter card with a quick explainer

scenes.narration: In the EloraTZP groups, A1C fell by 2.2 to 2.9 percentage points. That's roughly 24 to 32 mmol/mol.
scenes.retention_device: New stat on screen

scenes.narration: Tirzepatide alone lowered it by 2.4 points, about 26 mmol/mol. Placebo: just 0.3 points, about 3 mmol/mol.

visual.stat_label: A1C points, tirzepatide vs placebo (≈26 vs 3 mmol/mol)

scenes.retention_device: Side-by-side reveal with placebo

scenes.narration: So the combo's range sits on both sides of tirzepatide. Some doses came out a little higher, some a little lower, and no formal head-to-head test was reported.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the 'might surprise you' loop

scenes.narration: In other words, the big gap in weight loss turned into a much smaller gap in blood sugar: at most half a point, 2.9 versus 2.4, or about 5 mmol/mol. Tirzepatide on its own already brought A1C down a lot.
scenes.on_screen_text: Big weight gap, small A1C gap
scenes.retention_device: Counterintuitive insight with the exact gap

scenes.narration: That's a useful reality check. A more eye-catching weight number doesn't automatically make a much better blood-sugar result.

visual.myth: More weight loss means much better blood sugar
visual.fact: Here, A1C drops were close: 2.2–2.9 vs 2.4 points

scenes.retention_device: Myth vs fact card

scenes.narration: Which brings us to the fine print. And this is where the story really turns.
scenes.retention_device: Cliffhanger into the key section

scenes.narration: Remember that missing head-to-head test? The trial's main goal was EloraTZP versus placebo. The comparison with tirzepatide was a secondary goal, and in what's been released so far, there's no statistical test of EloraTZP versus tirzepatide.
scenes.retention_device: Callback to the opening caveat

scenes.narration: So 23.3% and 14.8% are numbers sitting side by side, not a proven win. The difference may well be real, but a small Phase 2b trial isn't designed to prove it.

visual.fact: Numerical comparison only; no formal test reported

scenes.retention_device: Decodes the headline claim directly

scenes.narration: Headlines saying the combo 'beat' tirzepatide are getting ahead of the data.
scenes.retention_device: Punchy one-liner

scenes.narration: Now, side effects. Lilly reports that between 10.8% and 27.0% of people across the EloraTZP doses stopped treatment because of adverse events.

visual.stat_label: Stopped for adverse events, combo doses (Lilly)

scenes.retention_device: Big new stat at the turn

scenes.narration: In the tirzepatide group, that figure was 2.9%. With eloralintide alone, it was 0% to 10.8%.
scenes.retention_device: Side-by-side contrast across arms

scenes.narration: Even the low end of the combo range is more than 3 times the tirzepatide figure. At the high end, it's more than 1 in 4 people.
scenes.retention_device: Vivid comparison

scenes.narration: One oddity: Lilly lists placebo discontinuation for adverse events at 16.7%, which is unusually high for a placebo group. With roughly 30 to 40 people per group, that's only a handful of people, so wait for the full paper before reading much into it.
scenes.on_screen_text: Placebo 16.7%? Small groups, wait for the paper
scenes.retention_device: 'Here's where it gets weird' moment

scenes.narration: Lilly says the most common side effects in this trial were gut-related, generally mild or moderate, and mostly during dose increases. They were more common with the combo. We don't yet have the breakdown of which side effects drove the stops. In tirzepatide and CagriSema trials, the usual ones were nausea, diarrhea, vomiting and constipation.
scenes.retention_device: Helpful context with a list visual

scenes.narration: And now, the payoff I promised. The detail that could matter more than the 23.3% itself.
scenes.retention_device: Main open loop pays off

scenes.narration: It comes down to one question: who gets counted in the average? Trials can calculate weight loss in different ways, called estimands.

visual.stock_query: people counted on a tally board

scenes.retention_device: Reveals the hidden detail as a question

scenes.narration: One counts everyone who was randomized, whether they stayed on the drug or not. Another estimates what happens if people stay on treatment as planned. That second one usually looks better.

items: Everyone randomized, stayed on or not
Estimated as if people stayed on treatment

scenes.retention_device: Clear explainer of a concept most viewers have never heard

scenes.narration: Lilly reports the 23.3% using the second approach, the 'if everyone had stayed on treatment' estimate. We couldn't find the count-everyone figure in the release. And when up to 27% of a group stopped early because of side effects, that choice can noticeably move the headline.
scenes.retention_device: Ties the main loop back to the dropout stat

scenes.narration: So the real Phase 3 question isn't just 'can it beat 14.8%?' It's 'can people stay on it long enough to get there?'
scenes.retention_device: Reframes the whole story; opens the 'what's next' loop

scenes.narration: A medicine only helps if you can keep taking it. That's the number to watch.
scenes.retention_device: Memorable takeaway line

scenes.narration: So what happens now? Lilly says it plans to start Phase 3 trials of an optimized co-formulation, with both drugs combined, by the end of 2026.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter card with a dated promise

scenes.narration: Phase 3 trials are usually much larger and longer, and they're designed to formally test whether one treatment does better than another. That's where 23.3% versus 14.8% either holds up or doesn't.
scenes.retention_device: Sets up a future payoff

scenes.narration: Until then, EloraTZP is investigational. It isn't approved, and the only legitimate way to receive it is inside a clinical trial.
scenes.retention_device: Clear status statement

scenes.narration: So if you ever see eloralintide sold online, as a 'research chemical' or anything else, skip it. That's not an approved medicine, and you can't know what's in the vial.

visual.fact: It's investigational and not approved; skip online sellers

scenes.retention_device: Safety myth-bust

scenes.narration: And if you take tirzepatide today, nothing about this trial changes your treatment. Tirzepatide's results come from large Phase 3 trials, and those still stand.
scenes.retention_device: Reassurance for the core audience

scenes.narration: So how do you make sense of the next big headline like this? Here's a 5-point checklist.
scenes.retention_device: Open loop: a promised checklist

scenes.narration: One: check the dose. 23.3% was the top combo dose, not every dose.
scenes.retention_device: Numbered checklist pacing

scenes.narration: Two: check who was studied. This trial was in adults with type 2 diabetes plus overweight or obesity. Results in other groups may differ.
scenes.retention_device: Numbered checklist pacing

scenes.narration: Three: look for a real head-to-head test. Numbers side by side aren't a proven win.
scenes.retention_device: Numbered checklist pacing

scenes.narration: Four: find the dropout rate. More people stopped the combo than tirzepatide because of side effects, and that matters as much as the average.
scenes.retention_device: Numbered checklist pacing

scenes.narration: Five: check the phase. Phase 2b means promising, not proven.
scenes.retention_device: Checklist recap card

scenes.narration: If you're curious whether amylin-based treatments or a clinical trial could fit you someday, that's a great question to bring to your next appointment.
scenes.retention_device: Empowering next step

scenes.narration: And if you're already on tirzepatide or another GLP-1 medicine, ask your care team how to protect muscle and make side effects easier. Those basics matter whatever comes next.
scenes.on_screen_text: Ask about muscle and side effects
scenes.retention_device: Practical takeaway for current users

scenes.narration: A quick reminder about tirzepatide and the other GLP-1 medicines on the market today: It's a prescription medicine. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.
scenes.retention_device: Required prescriber line

scenes.narration: Lilly says Phase 3 should start by the end of 2026, and we'll decode those results when they land. Subscribe to InforMed, and you'll get the real numbers, fine print included, before the hype sets in.
scenes.retention_device: CTA tied to a specific future payoff

factcheck.summary:
I checked the script against Lilly's 30 Sept 2026 release (S1) and HCPLive (S2). Every EloraTZP number in the script matches them:
- 367 adults with type 2 diabetes plus overweight or obesity, at sites in the US and Argentina, over 48 weeks.
- Double-blind trial with 10 groups (about 37 per group).
- Average starting weight 105.4 kg (232.4 lb) and starting A1C 8.1%.
- Weight loss: combo 13.2–23.3% (top dose eloralintide 9 mg plus tirzepatide 15 mg), tirzepatide 15 mg 14.8%, eloralintide alone 8.2–12.3%, placebo 3.0%.
- A1C drop: combo 2.2–2.9 points, tirzepatide 2.4, placebo 0.3.
- Stopped because of side effects: combo 10.8–27.0%, eloralintide 0–10.8%, tirzepatide 2.9%, placebo 16.7%.
- Gut side effects were mostly during dose increases and more common with the combo. Phase 3 of a co-formulation is planned by the end of 2026.

Lilly's release gives only the 'if everyone stayed on treatment' estimate (efficacy estimand) and no statistical test against tirzepatide, so the script's main point is accurate.

The comparison figures from other trials also check out:
- SURMOUNT-2 'if they stayed on treatment' estimate: 15.7% at the top dose vs 3.3% placebo, from Lilly's 2023 release. The figures counting everyone are 14.7% vs 3.2%.
- SURMOUNT-1: 20.9% vs 3.1%.
- REDEFINE 2 (CagriSema): 13.7% vs 3.4% over 68 weeks, counting everyone.
- The mmol/mol conversions are correct.

Safety framing is strong: it says the drug is investigational and only available in trials, warns against buying it online, says nothing changes for people already on tirzepatide, and includes the exact prescriber line.

The remaining issues are minor wording and source-label fixes:
- The tirzepatide comparison was a secondary endpoint.
- One cited source title has words added that aren't in the real title.
- One placebo figure needs its counting method named.
- One scene cites S1 for something S1 doesn't say.

I couldn't open the NEJM, ADA and Pharmacological Reviews pages (blocked or redirected). Search results and their known publication details confirm they exist.

thumbnail.reasoning: All three clear the legibility bar (≥7). #1 (\"AMYLIN BOOST?\" versus layout) best matches the title's head-to-head framing (eloralintide+tirzepatide vs tirzepatide alone), uses contrasting mascot expressions (worried vs happy) for emotional pull, and keeps a single clear comparison as the focal point — the strongest combination of curiosity and clarity. #0 is a close second with a good curiosity hook but a tiny top badge and competing text sizes. #2 is the cleanest and most legible but is the most generic/least tied to the specific numeric comparison the title promises, so it likely underperforms on CTR despite perfect readability.
